web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Price Is What It Is — Reverse DCF, Multiple Re-Rating & Peer Economics
question: What growth, margin durability, and reinvestment rate is the market already pricing into GHFL at ₹7,522.50 (41.0x TTM P/E), and how does that compare with domestic film peers?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get—and a reverse DCF tells you the exact expectations you are underwriting before you buy a single share.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Principle

web_blocks.title: 7.1 Market-Implied Expectations: Enterprise Value & Reverse DCF at ₹7,522.50

web_blocks.html: At the audited November 13, 2026 NSE session close of ₹7,522.50 (note that TradingView's intraday/delayed feed printed ₹7,647.50, whereas the verified exchange close is ₹7,522.50), Garware Hi-Tech Films has a market cap of ₹17,472 Cr across 2.323 Cr shares [1, 24]. Subtracting ₹920 Cr of net cash leaves an Enterprise Value (EV) of roughly ₹16,552 Cr [1, 11]. That net cash comprises ₹813 Cr in investments and ₹120 Cr in bank cash against ₹13 Cr of debt as of September 2026 [1, 11]. On TTM numbers through September 2026 (₹2,384 Cr sales, ₹547 Cr operating EBITDA, ₹426 Cr PAT; TTM EPS ₹183.41), the stock trades at 41.0x TTM P/E and 30.3x TTM EV/EBITDA [1]. It also trades at 6.94x EV/Sales and 6.01x Price-to-Book (book value ₹1,251/share, dividend yield 0.16%) [1].

To see what this price demands, we invert the DCF model. We use a 12.0% cost of equity (WACC ~12.0%), a 10-year forecast, and a 5.5% terminal growth rate (16.0x exit EV/FCF). At an EV of ₹16,552 Cr, GHFL must compound Free Cash Flow at 18.5% to 20.0% per year over the next decade. That takes FCF from ₹114 Cr in FY26 (or ₹250–₹280 Cr normalized) to ₹1,400–₹1,550 Cr by FY36 [1, 11]. In sales and profit terms, it implies 14%–16% annual sales growth and 24%–26% steady EBITDA margins with tight working capital. In short, the market no longer prices GHFL like a packaging converter. It prices in a durable specialty compounder backed by TPU and solar-film growth [5, 13].

web_blocks.caption: GRWRHITECH: Reverse DCF Sensitivity — Implied 10-Year FCF & Revenue CAGR at EV ₹16,552 Cr
rows: Upside if H1 FY27 margins (28.7%) hold
web_blocks.takeaway: At 30.3x TTM EV/EBITDA, ₹7,522.50 prices in ~15% revenue CAGR and 25% sustainable EBITDA margins; upside requires either faster SCF/PPF volume ramp or durable 27–28% margins from TPU backward integration [1, 5, 11].

web_blocks.title: 7.2 Historical Re-Rating, Forward Multiple Compression & Sum-of-the-Parts Lens

web_blocks.html: Over the past year, GHFL shares rallied +113.98% from a 52-week low of ₹2,690.70 to ₹7,522.50 (6.89% below the ₹8,079.50 high) [1, 24]. Five years ago, commodity BOPET dragged margins down and the market priced GHFL at 10x–15x earnings. The re-rating to 41.0x TTM P/E reflects two shifts: VAP hit 86–87% of sales, and H1 FY27 PAT jumped to ₹262 Cr (₹524 Cr annualized) [8, 11, 21]. On forward estimates of ₹530–₹560 Cr in FY27E and ₹640–₹690 Cr in FY28E, the P/E drops from 41.0x TTM to 32.0x FY27E and 26.2x FY28E [5, 11, 13]. Stripping out ₹920 Cr of net cash (₹396/share) puts the core business at ₹7,126.50/share, or ~24.8x FY28E earnings. That forward compression makes the price defensible if execution holds.

web_blocks.title: 7.3 Domestic Peer Comparison: Specialty Brand vs. Commodity Converters

web_blocks.html: Comparing GHFL with Indian polymer peers shows why its higher multiple is structural, not random. Pure packaging film makers sit trapped in BOPP/BOPET supply gluts with weak returns [1, 24]. Cosmo First trades at 10.1x P/E and 1.23x P/B with 7.13% OPM and 11.2% ROCE, while Polyplex posts 20.17x P/E, 3.85% OPM, and 0.89% ROCE [1, 24]. Jindal Poly Films is loss-making (-34.8% OPM, -1.99% ROCE), and Ester Industries earns 4.97% OPM and 2.75% ROCE [1, 24]. Only specialty chemical leader SRF (32.16x P/E, 4.80x P/B, 18.79% OPM, 14.6% ROCE) comes close [1, 24]. Even SRF faces cyclical packaging headwinds, whereas GHFL's PPF and SCF units deliver 23%–28% EBITDA margins and 18.1% ROCE [1, 11].

web_blocks.caption: NSE Polymer & Specialty Film Peer Valuation and Profitability Snapshot (as of 2026-11-13)
web_blocks.takeaway: GRWRHITECH commands the highest P/E (41.0x) and P/B (6.01x) in the group because its 20.87%–23% operating margin and 18.1% ROCE dwarf commodity BOPET/BOPP converters [1, 24].

web_blocks.company: Supreme Industries Ltd (Pipe & Polymer Re-Rating, India)
web_blocks.mechanism: Once valued as a 12x–16x PVC pipe maker, Supreme shifted into CPVC and engineered polymer systems with net cash and 20%+ ROCE. Brand reach and SKU depth buffered raw-material swings, driving a lasting re-rating to 35x–45x earnings.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: From FY14 to FY24, Supreme grew sales at ~11% CAGR and PAT at ~15% CAGR. Its market cap rose 7x (from ~₹6,500 Cr to >₹50,000 Cr) as P/E expanded from ~16x to >45x.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Once a polymer firm crosses 80%+ value-added mix with net cash, multiples rarely fall back to 12x unless margins crack. GHFL's 30x–42x band can hold if 24%+ OPM lasts, though entry discipline still favors buying dips.

web_blocks.title: 7.4 Capital Allocation & The Treasury Cash Discount

web_blocks.html: A subtle point in GHFL's valuation is its ₹933 Cr cash and investment pile, equal to 5.3% of its ₹17,472 Cr market cap [1, 11]. Dividend payout has stayed low at 8% of PAT (0.16% yield), while treasury funds earn ~8%–9% pre-tax [1]. As a result, the market applies a mild cash-drag discount to idle cash versus factory assets [1]. Higher payouts or buybacks after the ₹191 Cr SCF capex wraps up in H1 FY28 would add a fresh catalyst [13]. Meanwhile, EV/IC sits near 7.8x on core operating capital ex-cash, reflecting strong returns on new film lines.

Cross-checking EV/Sales and PEG points to the same discipline. GHFL trades at 6.94x trailing EV/Sales and 41.0x TTM P/E against a 22% 5-year PAT CAGR [1, 11]. Against 20%–24% projected FY26–FY28E PAT growth, that puts the forward PEG at 1.2x–1.4x [1, 11]. The stock is neither a hidden bargain nor a bubble—entry price decides your return.

What Would Change This Call: A dip into the lower-to-mid half of ₹7,156.51–₹7,525.07 (₹7,156.51–₹7,350.00) improves on the 1.81:1 base asymmetry at ₹7,522.50 and triggers staged limit buys; conversely, a sustained drop in operating margins below 20% or a weekly close below ₹6,515.60 breaks the reverse-DCF base case and invalidates the buy thesis.

book_paragraphs: For six chapters, we deliberately kept our eyes off the stock ticker. We wanted to know whether Garware Hi-Tech Films was a real specialty compounder before we let the market's enthusiasm or skepticism color our judgment. Now that the business has earned a COMPOUNDER_PASS on its fundamentals, it is time to open the quote screen and ask the hardest question in investing: at ₹7,522.50 per share, what has the market already priced in?

Let's do the arithmetic cleanly. At the audited November 13, 2026 NSE session close of ₹7,522.50—note that TradingView's intraday/delayed feed printed ₹7,647.50—Garware's market capitalization stands at ₹17,472 crore across 2.323 crore shares. After subtracting ₹920 crore of net cash—composed of ₹933 crore in cash and treasury investments against just ₹13 crore of borrowings as of September 2026—the enterprise value is roughly ₹16,552 crore. Against trailing-twelve-month revenue of ₹2,384 crore, operating EBITDA of ₹547 crore, and net profit of ₹426 crore through September 2026 (TTM EPS ₹183.41), you are paying 41.0 times trailing earnings, 30.3 times trailing EBITDA, 6.94 times sales, and 6.01 times book value.

Nobody pays 41 times earnings by accident. When we run a reverse discounted cash flow model at a 12% cost of equity and a 5.5% terminal growth rate—equivalent to a 16-times terminal free-cash-flow exit multiple—an enterprise value of ₹16,552 crore tells us the market expects Garware to compound free cash flow at roughly 19% annually over the next decade. Translated into factory terms, that means growing revenue at around 15% a year while defending 25% operating margins and keeping working capital under control. In other words, the easy multiple expansion from a 12-times-earnings commodity polyester company to a 40-times-earnings specialty brand has already happened during this year's 114% rally.

Does that automatically make the stock overvalued? Not necessarily, because trailing numbers lag an inflecting income statement. In the first half of FY27 alone, Garware earned ₹262 crore in net profit—an annualized run-rate above ₹520 crore—thanks to surging PPF adoption and the margin lift from its new TPU extrusion line. On realistic FY28 earnings estimates of ₹640 to ₹690 crore, once the ₹191 crore solar-control film expansion contributes, the forward multiple compresses into the mid-twenties. Stripping out ₹396 per share of net cash brings the core operating business down to roughly 24.8 times FY28 earnings—still not cheap, and leaving zero room for an export or tariff stumble, which is why disciplined entry matters.

book_subsections.title: Why Garware Trades at 41x While Packaging Film Peers Trade at 10x
paragraphs: If you glance at a domestic peer table without reading Chapters 2 through 4, Garware's valuation looks absurd. Cosmo First trades at 10.1 times earnings and 1.23 times book value. Polyplex trades at 20.2 times depressed earnings with a 3.85% operating margin and less than 1% ROCE. Jindal Poly Films is posting negative operating margins of minus 34.8%, and Ester Industries earns under 3% on capital. Why would any sane investor pay four times Cosmo First's multiple for Garware?

The answer is that Garware is no longer competing in their industry. Commodity BOPET and BOPP packaging films suffer from brutal Chinese and domestic capacity waves that crush margins every three years, turning every boom into a bust. Garware's 87% value-added mix—led by automotive paint protection films and architectural solar-control films sold through global distributors and Garware Application Studios—generates 21% to 28% operating margins and an 18.1% ROCE, closer to specialty chemical leader SRF (32.2x P/E, 18.8% OPM) than to packaging converters.

We saw a similar structural re-rating in India's Supreme Industries between 2014 and 2024. Investors once anchored Supreme to a 15-times PVC pipe multiple, missing how its shift toward higher-margin CPVC and engineered polymer systems—combined with a net-cash balance sheet—permanently lifted its valuation band above 35 to 45 times earnings. From FY14 to FY24, Supreme compounded revenue at 11% and profits at 15%, yet its market value multiplied sevenfold because the market stopped treating it as a commodity converter. That history teaches us not to short or dismiss Garware merely because its P/E starts with a four—but it also warns us that at 41.0x trailing earnings, future returns must come from earnings growth rather than further multiple expansion.

book_subsections.title: What Breaks the Valuation Model—and What Unlocks Upside
paragraphs: Every reverse DCF has two pressure points: margin durability and reinvestment runway. Look at our sensitivity table. If Garware's operating margins slip back to 20% because of U.S. tariff friction or aggressive Chinese PPF discounting, the market-implied revenue growth jumps above 18% per year just to justify today's enterprise value—an unrealistic bar that would force the multiple down toward 22 to 25 times earnings. Conversely, if the Lubrizol-partnered TPU line and the 1,200 LSF solar-control expansion allow Garware to hold 26% to 28% EBITDA margins while growing revenue 14% to 16% annually, then ₹16,552 crore is not a ceiling at all—it is a stepping stone toward ₹21,000 crore-plus over the next 18 months.

There is also a third, quieter lever sitting right on the balance sheet: capital allocation. Today, Garware holds ₹933 crore in cash and treasury investments—roughly ₹396 per share, or more than 5% of the entire market capitalization—while paying out just 8% of net profit in dividends. Treasury funds earning 8% pre-tax are safe, but they dilute headline ROE and invite a mild cash-drag discount from institutional investors. Once the ₹191 crore solar-control expansion finishes in H1 FY28, management will generate even more surplus cash.

Think about what happens if the board pairs its operational compounding with a formal capital-return policy—either lifting the dividend payout toward 20% to 25% or executing opportunistic share buybacks. That single step would lift headline ROE closer to factory ROCE and narrow any valuation discount relative to premier specialty chemical peers like SRF. Until then, our valuation discipline remains straightforward: respect the 41.0x trailing P/E, recognize the forward compression into the mid-twenties by FY28, and insist on buying pullbacks rather than chasing peak extensions.

book_subsections.title: How to Use Trailing vs. Forward Multiples Without Fooling Yourself
paragraphs: One of the easiest traps in growth investing is using forward earnings estimates to excuse paying any price today. When analysts say a stock at 41.0 times trailing earnings is really only 26.2 times FY28 earnings, they are implicitly assuming two full years of flawless execution—no U.S. tariff disruption, no raw-material spike, no delay in the ₹191 crore solar-control line, and no working-capital blowup.

That is why we anchor our valuation work in both directions. First, we check the trailing reality: 30.3 times TTM EBITDA and 6.94 times sales leave zero margin for error if H2 FY27 stumbles. Second, we check the forward trajectory: H1 FY27 already delivered ₹262 crore of net profit, proving that the 28.7% EBITDA margin inflection is showing up in audited quarterly results rather than PowerPoint slides. Balancing those two truths keeps us from being either too cynical to own a genuine winner or too reckless to wait for a fair entry price.

To put the valuation in one final perspective, imagine buying an unlisted specialty polymer plant that earns 25% operating margins, holds ₹920 crore of net cash, and grows 15% a year. In private equity, you would expect to pay 20 to 25 times EBITDA for that asset. In public markets, liquidity, scarcity value in Indian specialty films, and the optionality of Garware's global distribution network push that multiple to 30.3 times trailing EBITDA—or roughly 25 times forward FY28 EBITDA. That is a fair price for quality, not a bargain-basement steal, which is precisely why our next chapter turns to the price chart to find a disciplined entry.

Let's also check the PEG ratio—price-to-earnings divided by growth—because growth investors often lean on it as a sanity check. Over the past five years, Garware compounded net profit at 22% annually, and if TPU backward integration plus the new solar-control line deliver 20% to 24% annual profit growth through FY28, the forward PEG ratio sits around 1.2 to 1.4 times. That is healthy for a debt-free specialty manufacturer, provided margins stay above 24%. Notice the recurring theme: valuation gives us permission to own Garware, but only if we respect the risk of paying peak multiples after a 114% run.

Finally, consider how the market values Garware's invested capital. On core operating capital excluding treasury investments, Enterprise Value to Invested Capital sits near 7.8 times—a clear reflection of the 25%-plus pre-tax returns generated by its Waluj and Chikalthana specialty lines. In specialty materials, high EV-to-invested-capital is sustainable only when barriers to entry protect pricing power; our blind audit in Chapters 3 and 4 showed that OEM approvals, multi-layer coating IP, and the 300-plus Garware Application Studios provide exactly that protection.

One practical way to stress-test this valuation is to ask what happens if Garware merely hits consensus-like mid-teens revenue growth with a 24% operating margin over the next two years, while its P/E multiple compresses from 41.0 times down to 33 times. Under those assumptions, FY28 earnings of roughly ₹650 crore still support a market capitalization above ₹21,400 crore—meaning earnings growth alone absorbs an eight-turn multiple contraction and still delivers a low-twenties total return. That is why we do not fear the optical 41.0x trailing P/E, yet we refuse to chase above support.

Of course, the converse is equally true, and that is why we keep our eyes wide open. If U.S. tariff friction returns or Chinese PPF producers undercut prices in Europe and India, a margin slide from 24% down to 19% would squeeze FY28 earnings toward ₹450 crore and pull the market multiple down toward 22 to 25 times—resulting in a ₹10,575 crore market cap, or roughly 39.5% downside from today's quote. Knowing both sides of that valuation seesaw before you commit capital is the difference between underwriting a business and gambling on momentum. When you stage bids inside the lower-to-mid half of our support zone, you give yourself a wide cushion against that downside.

book_callouts.title: The Valuation Bottom Line at ₹7,522.50
book_callouts.text: The market is pricing in ~15% annual revenue growth and 25% durable EBITDA margins over the next decade. Future returns from CMP depend on operational compounding (TPU backward integration and the H1 FY28 SCF expansion) rather than further P/E expansion.
